title: Otis and the Midnight Cat
markdown:
Otis was a young wizard. He could make teacups do a little jig and dust bunnies perform a rather impressive synchronized swimming routine. One thing made his knees wobble more than a jelly tower in an earthquake: being alone. Especially alone in the deep quiet dark. He often muttered to his spellbooks that silence could be quite loud. It hummed with all the things that were not there. He would tap his chin, brow furrowed like a well-ploughed field. Even the rustle of his own robes sounded like a dragon’s whisper in the stillness.

One blustery afternoon Madame Evangeline, the famous potion maker from the village, hurried into Otis’s tower. Her apron was splattered with a rainbow of colourful spills, and she smelled of cinnamon and star anise. “Otis, my dear boy,” she boomed, voice like warm honey and lavender. “I have a most important errand. A rather special mix of giggling gas needs supervising, and I need a skilled wizard to pet-sit Alistair for just one evening.” She gestured to a creature as dark as midnight. Alistair. A cat who looked as though he had swallowed a thundercloud and was rather pleased about it. Fur the colour of a forgotten night sky, slick and glossy. Emerald eyes that seemed to know where you had hidden your best spell-ink, and frankly approved. A low rumble, like distant thunder, came from his chest.

Otis’s heart did a little flip-flop, a frantic butterfly in his ribcage. Pet-sit. A cat. Alone. In his tower. His fingers twisted the hem of his robe. “Oh, I… I suppose I could,” he stammered, voice a little thin. “As long as he doesn’t do anything too active. Or make too much noise. Or look at me for too long.” He imagined the cat’s steady gaze, a silent judgment on every nervous twitch.

Madame Evangeline chuckled, pebbles in a tin can, but with a warmth that eased the worry slightly. “Alistair is a creature of habit. He’ll sleep most of the night, dreaming of mice and perhaps the meaning of life, who knows. Just make sure he has his cream. And perhaps a nice sunny spot for his naps.” She winked. “He’s a good boy, really. Just particular.” And with a flurry of goodbyes and a look that seemed to say don’t worry too much, she was gone, leaving a faint trail of lavender.

Otis found himself in his tower, the heavy oak door bolted with a satisfying thud, with only the steady tick-tock of the grandfather clock and a very judgy-looking cat for company. The silence began to press in, a heavy blanket muffling the world outside and making the smallest creaks and groans of the old tower seem much louder. He tried to focus on his new levitation charm, picturing a feather dancing in the air, but his eyes kept darting to Alistair. The cat was curled on the wide sun-drenched windowsill, a dark comma against the bright afternoon light, twitching the tip of his tail in a rhythm that felt almost mocking. Suddenly, with a sound like a sigh of a very bored cat, Alistair stretched. He yawned, a cavernous pink maw revealing tiny sharp teeth, and then, quick as a whisper, he was out. Through the open window.

“Alistair,” Otis yelped, scrambling to the sill. His heart leaped into his throat. Night air, suddenly cool, smelling of damp earth, crushed pine needles, and the faintest hint of distant woodsmoke, rushed in. He peered down. In the faint moonlight already beginning to paint the world silver and grey, Alistair was a dark silhouette, trotting with a sure-of-himself walk toward the whispering woods that bordered the property.

“Oh, no, no, no,” Otis muttered, stomach doing a somersault. He could not leave Alistair. What if he got lost? What if something in the woods made a noise that sounded like a monster? He grabbed his warmest cloak, wool thick and comforting, and a flickering lantern that cast wobbly dancing shadows on the stone walls. Out the door he went, chasing a vanishing black shape, red hair a bright streak against the darkening sky.

The trees stood tall and old, branches like long fingers reaching for the starry sky. The sky unfurled like a dark velvet blanket. The path, so familiar and welcoming in daytime, now twisted and turned, each root and stone a potential trip, the whole scene unfamiliar. Otis’s breath hitched. Rustle of leaves. Sharp hoot of an owl high above. Distant snap of a twig. Sounds that in his tower seemed distant and imaginary felt much closer here. He was truly alone, deeper in the woods than he had ever been, and the tick-tock of the clock was now a drumming in his ears, reminding him that midnight was fast approaching. Shadows seemed to stretch and warp. He imagined unseen things lurking just beyond the lantern’s feeble glow, eyes like tiny unfriendly stars.

Then, just as a shiver of true cold traced its way up his spine, Alistair stopped. He sat down as calmly as if he were on his favourite velvet cushion, by a gnarled oak whose roots snaked over the ground like sleeping dragons, and began to wash a paw with meticulous care. Otis, panting, stumbled toward him, lantern swinging wildly. “Alistair. You can’t just—” He stopped. Standing near the oak, hunched over a rickety cart overflowing with jewel-toned berries that seemed to hold their own inner light, was a goblin. Nose like a round beetroot, twitching with curiosity. A rather smart hat made of a large speckled mushroom cap.

The goblin peered at Otis with bright beady eyes that missed nothing. “Lost, little wizard? Or just admiring my moonberries? Rarest in the forest. Grown in moonbeams and dew, you see.” His voice was rough, pebbles stirred in a tin.

And here was the curious thing about Alistair, whom Otis had thought merely grumpy and aloof. The cat let out a low rumbling purr that sounded almost like a question directed at the goblin. The goblin tilted his head, mushroom hat wobbling. “Ah, you want to take the furry one home, do you? He’s a wise one, that cat. Knows more than he lets on. Been asking about the moonpetal bloom, he has.”

Otis stared, jaw slightly ajar. Alistair… communicating? With a goblin? “He… he wants to go home?” he managed, barely a whisper, disbelief and a dawning wonder mixed.

The goblin nodded, hat wobbling again. “He does. But the moon will be too high soon for easy passage. To get him back safely, and without any undue fuss, you’ll need a moonpetal. They only bloom when the moon is at its highest, by the Whispering Falls. Tricky to find, mind you. The falls sing secrets to those who listen.”

The Whispering Falls. Even deeper into the woods, a place rumoured to be filled with trickster sprites and rustling shadows. The old fear tried to claw back, a cold knot in his stomach. Then his shoulders straightened. The knot loosened, replaced by a steady warmth. He looked at Alistair, then at the goblin, and a small determined smile touched his lips. “We’ll find it,” he said, voice steadier and clearer than he had expected. “Show us the way, please.”

The goblin grunted, slow approval, and pointed a knobbly finger deeper into the trees, where moonlight seemed to gather in pools. “Follow the winding stream. Keep your wits about you, and the cat. He knows the way, more than you think.”

They went. Alistair trotted ahead, tail held high like a proud banner, a beacon of quiet confidence in the deepening gloom. Otis followed closely, lantern out, steps more sure now. The woods seemed to whisper secrets, not threats. Gentle murmur of the stream, a soothing lullaby. Silvery glint of moonlight on dew-kissed leaves, like scattered diamonds. He even managed a small hopeful smile when a particularly large shiny beetle scuttled across their path. Still a little nervous, yes, but it was not the overwhelming dread from before. More like a gentle tingle, an invitation.

They reached a small clearing bathed in the soft glow of the moon. Beside a waterfall that tumbled down rocks like bright moonlight were the most delicate pale blue flowers Otis had ever seen. They unfurled their petals softly, shimmering as if they held captured starlight. “Moonpetals,” he breathed. He gently touched one, cool and soft against his fingertips. They smelled faintly of rain and dreams.

As they turned to go, Alistair rubbed against Otis’s leg with a surprisingly affectionate purr that vibrated through him. Otis knelt and scratched behind his ears, sleek fur and rumbling contentment. “You know, Alistair,” he whispered, “you’re not so grumpy after all.”

They made their way back through woods that now felt familiar, the moon directly overhead, everything in a cool calm glow. The return felt quicker, less daunting, as if the forest itself had decided to help them home. As they stepped into the familiar warmth of Otis’s tower, the grandfather clock began to chime. Twelve solemn bongs, each note echoing. Midnight.

Otis looked at Alistair, now curled on the hearth rug, utterly content, emerald eyes half-closed. He had not been alone in the dark, not really. He had had a companion: grumpy, mysterious, loyal, and surprisingly sure-footed. The silence of the tower no longer felt loud or empty. It felt like a room that could hold a cat and a wizard and a lantern still faintly smelling of pine. He set out the cream. Alistair drank as if midnight were an ordinary hour. Otis left the window latched, but not because the dark was waiting. Because the cream was inside, and so were they.
